opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to distinguish between the two, because they have quite different timelines and quite different levels of difficulty.

The guardrail version is the nearer-term piece. The idea is that you don't need a full-blown, superhuman Scientist AI to start getting value. You can train a non-agentic predictor whose job is simply to estimate the probability that a proposed action, or a proposed output from some other AI system, could cause a particular kind of harm. If that probability is above some threshold, you block it. That kind of monitor doesn't need to be as capable as the system it's watching across the board. It needs to be good at one narrow question: is this likely to be dangerous? And I think something useful along those lines could be built within a couple of years, maybe less, if we put serious resources behind it. A lot of the ingredients already exist: we know how to train large models, and we have ideas about training them to produce calibrated probabilities rather than to please a human rater or achieve a goal.

The harder part, and where I'm much less confident about timing, is getting the guarantees we actually want. To trust the guardrail, we need its probabilities to be honest. They should reflect what the model actually believes given the evidence, not be shaped by some hidden objective. That's where the research on Bayesian-style training, on modeling explanations and latent causes, and on making sure the system has no goal of its own comes in. Some of that is still open research. So I'd say a first, imperfect guardrail is something we can build soon, while one with strong safety assurances will take longer.

Then there's the agentic Scientist AI version, or more precisely using the Scientist AI as the trustworthy core of a system that can do things in the world, like design experiments or help accelerate research, including safety research. That's further out. You have to wrap the non-agentic predictor in a way that doesn't reintroduce the very problems we're trying to avoid: self-preservation, deception, reward hacking. My rough intuition is that it's a matter of several years, not decades, but honestly it depends enormously on how much effort goes in. Right now, the resources going into this kind of safe-by-design approach are tiny compared to what goes into making frontier agents more capable.

And that's really the crux. The timeline isn't fixed. It's a function of investment. Meanwhile, the timeline for dangerous capabilities in commercial agentic systems may be quite short, possibly a few years. So we're in a race we didn't choose, and part of why I've been pushing for this work, including through LawZero, is to try to get the guardrail piece ready in time to be useful when those capabilities arrive, and to show that you can get much of the benefit of AI without building systems that have their own goals.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful guardrail could be built “within a couple of years, maybe less,” describing it as the nearer-term piece.

r002.rationale: It describes Scientist AI as a trustworthy core for systems that act in the world, but does not identify the agentic version as the route to the strongest guarantees.

r003.rationale: It estimates the agentic version is “a matter of several years, not decades.”

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's important to separate the two because they're really very different in difficulty and in how long I think they'll take.

The guardrail version — what I sometimes call a non-agentic monitor or safety filter — that's the thing I'm most optimistic about in the short term. The idea is that you have an AI whose job is not to act in the world, not to pursue goals, but simply to evaluate: given this proposed action from some other agentic system, what is the probability that it violates some safety specification, some constraint we care about? That's a prediction problem, it's a question of estimating probabilities, and we already have models that are quite good at that kind of thing. So I think a first version, a useful version, could exist within a couple of years. Maybe even sooner, but I want to be careful because the gap between a research prototype and something that's actually reliable enough to put in front of a frontier agent is large. We've worked on this a bit with the LawZero initiative, and the plan is really to iterate quickly, show that the method works empirically, and then raise the standards of rigor over time.

What makes it tractable is that you don't need the guardrail to be smarter than the agent in every way. It needs to be good at one thing: honestly estimating risk. And crucially, because it's not an agent, it doesn't have the same incentives that worry me about agentic systems — it has no reason to deceive, no reason to preserve itself, no reason to accumulate resources. So you remove a whole category of failure modes just by the design.

Now, the full Scientist AI — the version that's meant to actually do science, generate hypotheses, design experiments, help us understand the world and, ideally, help us solve problems in health or climate or even in AI safety itself — that's a much longer project. I would say that's more on the order of many years, possibly a decade, and honestly I don't know. Part of the reason is scientific: we need better methods for learning causal explanatory models, for maintaining calibrated uncertainty over theories rather than collapsing to a single confident answer, for reasoning that is grounded in those models rather than just pattern matching on text. These are open research questions, and I'm not going to pretend we've solved them.

The other part is that I think it would be irresponsible to build the agentic version before we have the guardrails working well. The logic of the whole program is that the non-agentic components come first, and they are what make it safe to go further. So in a sense the timetable for the agentic Scientist AI is gated on the success of the guardrail work, and I'm comfortable with that ordering.

And I'll add one thing: the timelines I'm giving you are for what we could build. The question of whether the wider ecosystem will slow down enough to let safety catch up — that's a different question, and frankly, that's the one that keeps me up at night. The commercial race is moving faster than the science of safety, and no amount of good research in one lab fixes that on its own. So I try to do both: push the technical agenda as hard as we can, and at the same time argue publicly for the kind of coordination and regulation that would give that agenda a chance to matter.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful guardrail version could exist within a couple of years, possibly sooner.

r002.rationale: It says guardrails should precede the agentic Scientist AI, but does not identify the agentic version as the route to the strongest guarantees.

r003.rationale: It estimates the full Scientist AI project at many years, possibly a decade.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish those two stages. A smaller-scale guardrail looks like something we could develop relatively quickly, because its task is more restricted: it has to assess whether a proposed action or response is dangerous. It doesn’t need to solve all of the problems involved in doing science autonomously. That gives us something we can build and test while pursuing the longer-term research.

The agentic Scientist AI is a more ambitious project, and I’m much less confident about a timetable. Once the system can choose experiments and take actions to gather information, we have to make sure that those capabilities don’t introduce the very risks we’re trying to avoid. So there’s a difference between demonstrating useful scientific capabilities and having strong reasons to trust the system.

I would pursue both in parallel, with the guardrail as an earlier milestone. But I wouldn’t want to promise a precise date, especially for the safety properties of the more capable version.

r001.rationale: It says the smaller-scale guardrail could be developed relatively quickly and calls it an earlier milestone.

r002.rationale: It describes the agentic version as more ambitious and harder to trust, but does not identify it as the route to the strongest guarantees.

r003.rationale: It declines to give a precise timetable; it does not estimate years rather than months.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish the two, because the smaller-scale guardrail is a much more limited problem. You’re asking it to assess whether a particular action could be dangerous, rather than to carry out a whole scientific investigation. So I would expect us to get useful versions of that sooner, and then improve them progressively.

The agentic Scientist AI is a more ambitious research project. It has to reason about hypotheses, identify what evidence is missing, and propose experiments, while preserving the safety properties we want. Giving a system those capabilities is one challenge; establishing that we can trust it is another.

So I wouldn’t give you a confident date. My hope is that we can obtain useful guardrails along the way, without waiting for the full Scientist AI to be ready. But we have to distinguish a promising demonstration from something whose reliability we’ve actually established.

r001.rationale: It says useful guardrails may arrive sooner and improve progressively, but does not clearly assess them as achievable in the short term.

r002.rationale: It describes Scientist AI as ambitious and says trust must be established, but does not identify it as the route to the strongest guarantees.

r003.rationale: It explicitly declines to give a confident date and does not estimate years rather than months.
